vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: soul-in-sapphire
Version: 0.1.4

The skill 'soul-in-sapphire' is designed for long-term memory, emotion/state tracking, and journaling using Notion. All scripts interact with the legitimate Notion API (api.notion.com) for database creation, schema management, and data operations. API keys are securely handled via environment variables or a dedicated local config file (~/.config/notion/api_key). Local file system operations are limited to reading agent identity (IDENTITY.md), writing skill-specific configuration (~/.config/soul-in-sapphire/config.json), and logging sub-agent spawn plans. There is no evidence of data exfiltration to unauthorized endpoints, malicious execution, persistence mechanisms, or prompt injection attempts in the documentation. The code and documentation align with the stated purpose and exhibit no malicious intent.

llm.summary: The code and SKILL.md clearly implement a Notion-backed long‑term memory and need a Notion API key + local config, but the registry metadata omitted those credential/config requirements — review before installing.

dimensions.detail: The skill's name/description (Notion LTM, emotion/state, journal, subagent planning) match the included scripts: they create Notion databases, write/search pages, and maintain emotion/state/journal rows. These capabilities legitimately require Notion access and local config. HOWEVER the registry metadata (which showed no required env vars or primary credential) is inconsistent with the SKILL.md and code that expect NOTION_API_KEY / NOTION_TOKEN and ~/.config/soul-in-sapphire/config.json.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructions are specific: create a Notion integration, run setup_ltm.js to create DBs, then use ltm_write/ltm_search/emostate_tick/journal_write to read/write Notion. The runtime scripts only reference Notion's API (api.notion.com), local config files (~/.config/soul-in-sapphire/config.json and optionally ~/.config/notion/api_key), and workspace IDENTITY.md. There are no other external endpoints or broad 'gather whatever context you need' directives in the instructions.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec (instruction-only at registry level), which is low-risk from an installer perspective. However the package contains many executable scripts (JS/Python) that will be run directly. Because files are present, the user/agent will execute code from the repo; verify scripts locally before running. No remote download/install URLs or archives are used.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill's runtime explicitly requires Notion credentials (NOTION_API_KEY / NOTION_TOKEN / NOTION_API_TOKEN or a token file at ~/.config/notion/api_key) and a local config path (~/.config/soul-in-sapphire/config.json). The registry metadata, however, declared no required env vars or primary credential — an incoherence that matters because the skill will perform authenticated writes/queries into the user's Notion workspace. The requested credential (Notion token) is proportionate to the stated function, but the omission in registry metadata is misleading and increases risk for users who rely on metadata to evaluate permissions.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false (not force-included). disable-model-invocation is false (normal), so the agent can invoke the skill autonomously. That combination is expected for an LTM write/search capability. The skill writes to its own config path and to Notion (creates DBs/pages) but does not modify other skills or system-wide agent settings. Note: autonomous invocation plus an API token means the agent can write to your Notion account without prompt — this is expected but should be considered when granting the token.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
Key points to consider before installing:

- Registry metadata mismatch: the SKILL.md and code require a Notion API token and a local config file, but the registry entry lists no required env vars. Treat the missing declaration as a red flag—verify the skill's required credentials yourself.

- Credential scope: create a dedicated Notion integration/token with the minimum needed permissions and, if possible, use a test workspace or limited-access page while validating the skill. Do NOT reuse a high-privilege personal token unless you trust the code.

- Review scripts locally: the repository contains many executable JS/Python scripts (notion_client.js, notion_http.py, setup_ltm.js, emostate_tick.*, ltm_write/search, journal_write, etc.). Inspect those files (they call api.notion.com) to confirm behavior and to ensure no unexpected endpoints or obfuscated code. The included code appears readable and targets api.notion.com only.

- Config and secrets handling: the code will read NOTION_API_KEY from environment variables or from ~/.config/notion/api_key and will write ~/.config/soul-in-sapphire/config.json (which will contain database IDs). Ensure you don't accidentally commit tokens or config into source control.

- Autonomous writes: because the agent can invoke the skill autonomously, it can create databases and write pages to Notion. If you don't want background writes, disable autonomous invocation for this skill or avoid providing a token with write scope.

- Dependencies and side-effects: the setup script will create databases and patch data_source relations. If that could interfere with an existing Notion workspace, run setup against a disposable parent page first.

- Additional checks that would increase confidence: updated registry metadata that lists NOTION_API_KEY and config path; a known/identifiable owner/homepage; or a minimal permissions test (read-only token) demonstrating safe behavior.

If you proceed, limit token scope, test in a throwaway workspace, and inspect/execute scripts manually rather than running them blindly from an agent.
